seo.title: Three MCP Features You Should Stop Building On
seo.hook: A lot of MCP writing online predates the current spec. Here's what actually changed.
seo.description: Eleven chapters reduce to one mental model: who is in control, and who is paying.

scenes.narration: A lot of MCP writing online predates the current spec. Here's what actually changed.

Here's the whole thing on one screen. Tools are functions the model chooses, and Claude never runs them — your code does, in the loop. Resources are data your code fetches, and injecting one beats a tool call whenever you already know what's needed. Prompts are workflows a person triggers, which is how you ship your own expertise as a button. Sampling reverses the protocol so the client's key pays, which is what makes a public server affordable. Roots are file access control that the S D K hands you but never enforces. And notifications are how a slow tool proves it's alive. Underneath all six, one question keeps working: who is in control — and for sampling, who is paying.

scenes.narration: Before you go and build, here's the state of play, because a lot of MCP writing online predates it. Tools, resources and prompts are current, and they're the spine of everything. Elicitation is current, and it's where the protocol is putting its weight now. Sampling is deprecated as of the twenty twenty six revision — migrate to calling a provider API directly. Roots is deprecated too — pass paths as tool parameters, resource U R Is, or server config instead. And logging is deprecated — standard error on stdio, Open Telemetry in production. None of those three vanish tomorrow. They stay in the spec for at least twelve months and the code you inherit will be full of them, which is exactly why you learnt them. Just don't start something new on a feature the specification has already told you it's retiring.
